passage: Saturday. I told Charu my biggest secret today: I'm scared of the dark, still, and I keep the hall light on at night. She didn't laugh. She said she sometimes checks under her bed. We giggled. Then she told me another secret, that her cousin scared her by saying he'd hide her shoes. I said, “That isn't okay, Charu, you should tell your mum.” She said she would think about it. I felt proud she trusted me. But Amma says some secrets are safe and some aren't; if a secret makes you feel scared, you tell a grown-up. So tonight I told Amma, and she rang Charu's mum straight away. Rekha.

qa.q: What does Charu sometimes check?
qa.a: Under her bed.

qa.q: Why did Rekha feel proud after the talk?
qa.a: Rekha felt proud that Charu trusted Rekha with a secret and did not laugh at the shared fear.

qa.q: What did Rekha say to Charu about the secret that made Charu scared?
qa.a: Rekha said it wasn't okay and Charu should tell her mum, because a secret that feels scary should be told to a grown-up.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt after sharing both secrets?
qa.a: Charu probably felt relieved and closer to a friend, though she was still unsure about telling her mum.

grounding: A child confides in a best friend, building trust, and learns that a secret that causes fear or harm should be told to a trusted adult.

passage: Under the mango tree at the edge of the field, Rehana whispered to Zainab, “I have not told anyone this. I failed my spelling test and hid the paper in my bag.” Zainab listened, then said, “I won't tell. But you might feel better if you show Ammi. She won't shout.” Rehana's lips trembled. “What if she does?” Zainab squeezed her hand. “I can come with you.” The two walked to Rehana's home in the afternoon sun. Rehana showed the paper. Her mother sighed, then hugged her. Zainab waited outside, smiling. Rehana called out, “Thank you for coming.”

qa.q: Where did the girls talk?
qa.a: Under the mango tree at the edge of the field.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she whispered her secret?
qa.a: She was worried and ashamed about the spelling test, which is why she hid it and her lips trembled when asked about her mother.

qa.q: What did Zainab do that helped Rehana?
qa.a: She kept the confidence, suggested showing Ammi and offered to walk with Rehana, so the secret was shared with a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Rehana's mother have felt on seeing the paper?
qa.a: She sighed, which may have been worry, then hugged her, so she seemed to care more about Rehana than the mark.

grounding: A child shares a secret with a best friend and is encouraged to tell a trusted adult.

passage: On the steps behind the school hall in Cape Town, Thabo told Omar something he hadn't told anyone. “I can't swim. Not really. I've been faking it in lessons, holding the rail.” Omar didn't laugh. “Is that why you always want to be last?” Thabo nodded, face hot. “Don't tell anyone.” Omar thought about it. “I won't. It's not a dangerous secret, just an embarrassing one.” Then he added, “But you could tell Coach. She could give you extra lessons, and no one would know why.” Thabo looked at his shoes. “Maybe.” The next week, Omar noticed Thabo staying late at the pool. He didn't ask. He just grinned.

qa.q: What had Thabo been doing in swimming lessons?
qa.a: Thabo had been faking it, holding the rail.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling when he told Omar?
qa.a: Thabo felt embarrassed, his face hot, but trusted Omar enough to share it.

qa.q: How did Omar decide whether to keep the secret?
qa.a: Omar thought about it and saw it wasn't dangerous, just embarrassing, so he kept it while gently suggesting Thabo tell the coach.

qa.q: What did Omar's grin at the pool show?
qa.a: It showed Omar was glad Thabo was getting help and that he had kept the secret without asking questions.

grounding: Shows a child confiding an embarrassing secret to a best friend, building trust, and the friend judging it safe to keep.

passage: After lights-out in the hostel dormitory, Sarika whispered across the gap between the beds. “Vinita, promise you won't tell? A Class 9 girl takes my snacks every night. She says if I tell anyone, she'll make sure I have no friends here.” Vinita sat up. She'd kept Sarika's other secrets, about her crush and about being scared of the dark. This one felt different. “Sarika, that's not a keep-it secret. She's threatening you. That's the kind we have to tell.” Sarika's voice shook. “Now?” “Now. I'll come with you.” They padded down the corridor to the warden's room. Ramya Ma'am listened, said none of it was Sarika's fault and let both girls sleep in the room beside hers. In the morning, she spoke to the Class 9 girl.

qa.q: Which class was the girl taking Sarika's snacks in?
qa.a: The girl was in Class 9.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling as she whispered the secret?
qa.a: Sarika felt scared and trapped by the older girl's threat, which is why her voice shook.

qa.q: How did Vinita tell this secret apart from the others?
qa.a: Vinita saw it involved a threat, so it was the kind of secret that must be told, and went with Sarika to the warden that night.

qa.q: How did Ramya Ma'am respond?
qa.a: She listened, said none of it was Sarika's fault, let both girls sleep near her that night and spoke to the older girl in the morning.

grounding: Shows a child confiding in a best friend, and the friend knowing that a secret about a threat must be told to a trusted adult at once.

passage: I'm Harish, Madhuri's brother. All week, Madhuri and her best friend Pihu sat on the terrace after school, heads together, whispering. When I came up, they went silent and giggled. I felt left out, and a bit suspicious. Were they talking about me? On Friday I asked Madhuri straight. “Is it a secret about me?” She laughed. “No! It's a good secret. A surprise kind.” Then she looked serious. “Ammi says there are two kinds: surprise secrets, which are fine, and secrets that make you scared, which you always tell. This one's a surprise.” On Sunday I found out: they'd been planning my birthday. I don't know everything they said up there, but I know Pihu kept it.

qa.q: What had Madhuri and Pihu been planning?
qa.a: They had been planning Harish's birthday.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when the girls went silent?
qa.a: Harish felt left out and a bit suspicious, wondering if they were talking about him.

qa.q: What rule about secrets did Madhuri explain?
qa.a: Surprise secrets are fine to keep, but secrets that make you scared must always be told.

qa.q: What did the whispering on the terrace show about Madhuri and Pihu?
qa.a: It showed trust between best friends, sharing and keeping a happy secret together.

grounding: Shows a child confiding in a best friend to build trust, and knowing which secrets are safe to keep and which must be told.

passage:
Monday: Behind the school water tank, Jaya whispered to Harsha that she practised her singing solo in the bathroom because the stage scared her. Harsha hooked her little finger. "Safe with me."
Thursday: Harsha didn't open his tiffin. "A big boy on the van takes my snack money. He said if I tell, I'll see." Jaya's stomach went cold. "This isn't a keep-it secret. Let's go now." At break they found Mrs Iyer, who listened to all of it and said, "It's not your fault, Harsha." Before home time she had called the van in-charge and Harsha's parents.
The next Monday: A teacher rode the van. Harsha sat in the front row of the hall, clapping loudest when Jaya sang.

qa.q: Where did Jaya first share her secret?
qa.a: Behind the school water tank.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when her stomach went cold?
qa.a: Jaya felt frightened for Harsha and alarmed, because unlike her own stage fear this secret was about someone being threatened.

qa.q: Why was Jaya right to treat the two secrets differently?
qa.a: Her stage fear harmed no one, so keeping it built trust; Harsha's secret involved threats and taken money, so it went to a trusted adult the same day.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt when Mrs Iyer said it was not his fault?
qa.a: Harsha likely felt relieved and less alone after being scared into silence by the threat.

grounding: It shows best friends building trust by sharing feelings, and one friend recognising that a secret about harm must go to a trusted adult straight away.
